source.title: Dynamics of neural scaling laws in random feature regression with powerlaw-distributed kernel eigenvalues
source.authors: Jakob Kramp; Javed Lindner; M. Helias

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study derives scaling behavior in random-feature regression and qualifies simple power-law descriptions with finite-size corrections and regime-specific assumptions.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own theoretical and simulation results for generalization error in a teacher-student random-feature regression model. It does not sweep language-model parameter count, pretraining tokens, or training compute. Results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is an analytical (dynamical mean-field) and simulation study of a linear teacher-student random-feature regression with synthetic Gaussian features and power-law eigenvalues. It derives power-law forms for bias, variance and early-stopped test error in P, N and t. It trains no language model, and no neural network on image, video or other real data. It reports no pretraining-loss sweeps, no extrapolation to larger runs, no compute-optimal split and no fitted exponents compared across setups. The results are a solvable-model account of why power laws can arise. They do not measure whether any version holds in the systems the versions name, so they are recorded under fits_no_version, not as verdicts.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that their dynamical mean-field theory captures typical-case generalization dynamics in kernel/random-feature regression. It unifies Bayesian inference, gradient flow with or without weight decay, and Langevin training. With power-law spectra it explains neural scaling laws as superpositions of mode-wise decays, and early stopping as a bias-variance trade-off. In the thermodynamic limit the optimal stopping time depends only on α and β, and the optimal error is a superposition of competing bias and variance power laws, with finite-size effects mattering in simulations.
record.recipe_differences: This is a theoretical and simulation study of linear teacher-student random-feature regression with Langevin training and generalization error, not a language-model pretraining sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The derived behavior depends on the kernel-spectrum exponent α, inverse temperature β, regularization, sample and system sizes P and N, and approximations such as neglecting disorder or retaining only the β-dependent variance contribution. The authors note finite-size effects and a difference from Bordelon et al. for finite P under their variance approximation.

fits_no_version.finding: In linear random-feature regression with power-law kernel spectrum η_i ∝ i^(-1-α) under Langevin training, bias error falls as (Pt)^(-α/(1+α)) with an N^-α finite-size correction. Variance grows as β^-1 P^(-α/(1+α)) t^(1/(1+α)). Early-stopped error scales as (Pβ)^(-α/(1+α)) - N^-α, and t* is independent of P and N. Simulations match approximately, and finite-size terms matter (Figs. 4–5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Solvable linear/kernel models with power-law feature spectra produce power-law test-error scaling in data, model size and training time, with exponents set by the spectral decay and finite-size corrections.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The results concern a linear random-feature regression model, not language models. Several scaling laws are derived under approximations and asymptotic assumptions; the paper itself notes finite-size effects. Simulations report disorder-average counts but no error bars or confidence intervals in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results omitted. Cited results from prior work were excluded.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss of language models versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation of fits from small runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal allocation of parameters versus tokens. The text only mentions that Eq. 34 corresponds to a Pareto frontier in f=6PNt, with no derived optimal split.
Depth, width or architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer settings for real neural models.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal split on parameter counting, schedule, data or fitting method in published laws.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T5' with V5/V7 support was rejected. V5 names neural models in other modalities or training regimes, and V7 concerns how published fits disagree; a synthetic linear toy model's derived asymptotics fit neither. R1's value is an OUP bound, which the text says the true bias decays slower than. The paper uses γ in Eq. 9 but α thereafter for the spectral exponent.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation from small language-model runs to much larger runs.
The compute-optimal allocation between model parameters and training tokens.
Comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Image and video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer; this study examines a linear random-feature regression setting, not those cases.
Downstream task performance and its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
The effects of alternative parameter-count conventions and fitting methods, and whether compute-optimal parameter/token allocations change across such choices.

rows.subject: random feature regression with powerlaw-distributed kernel eigenvalues
rows.size_stated: P, N >> 1; the finite-size expression includes N
rows.operation_detail: Derives the bias generalization-error scaling after replacing the random feature matrix by its expectation.
rows.measure: Bias part of generalization error L_bias
rows.value: L_bias,OUP ∼ c1(Pt)^(-α/(1+α)) - c2 N^(-α), with positive constants c1 and c2
rows.note: The leading power law is accompanied by a finite-N correction. The paper says that for finite system sizes the bias should be viewed as a superposition of power laws.
rows.check: Concerns a linear random-feature toy model, not language models or neural models in other modalities. Eq. 34 is the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck limit that neglects disorder in Q. The paper says the true bias decays slower than this, so it is a bound, not the bias itself. Fig. 4 reports simulations agreeing with the predicted power law plus a non-negligible N^-α correction.

rows.subject: random feature regression with powerlaw-distributed kernel eigenvalues
rows.size_stated: P, N >> 1; the derivation includes a finite-N correction
rows.operation_detail: Derives the high-temperature approximation for the variance contribution to generalization error.
rows.measure: Variance contribution L_β to generalization error
rows.note: The paper also gives finite-N correction terms in Appendix G.2. This is an asymptotic result under the stated approximation.
rows.check: A toy-model asymptotic for the variance term in the high-temperature (β→0) limit. This is a growing-with-time noise term, not held-out pretraining loss of any version's system.

rows.subject: random feature regression with powerlaw-distributed kernel eigenvalues
rows.size_stated: P and N are stated to be absent from the leading-order result
rows.operation_detail: Derives the stopping time that minimizes the generalization error in the stated approximation.
rows.note: The authors state that the stopping time is independent of P and N in the thermodynamic-limit result; simulations are shown for P = N = 100.
rows.check: Optimal early-stopping time t* = βα/[2(1+α)], independent of P and N. This is not a scaling of loss with parameters, data or compute, and it bears on no version.

rows.subject: random feature regression with powerlaw-distributed kernel eigenvalues
rows.size_stated: N appears in the finite-size term
rows.operation_detail: Derives the generalization error evaluated at the optimal stopping time.

conditions.value: high-temperature variance approximation and early stopping

rows.locator: Section 5.3, Eq. (37); Appendix G.3; Fig. 4 inset
rows.note: The authors describe finite-size effects as important for correctly estimating the optimal error. The stated law is an approximation with an explicit N-dependent correction.
rows.check: Early-stopped test error in the toy model, d1(Pβ)^(-α/(1+α)) - d2 N^-α. The paper says it holds 'approximately in simulations' with important finite-size effects (Fig. 4 inset). The system is not one named by any version.

relation.reason: It discusses neural scaling laws and their possible spectral explanation, while its own analytical and simulation results concern a fixed-feature linear teacher-student model.

tranche.reason: The study derives generalization dynamics for synthetic linear random-feature regression. Its results do not test the specified language-model or other neural-training claim versions, and it does not use an empirical scaling law as a tool.

source_check.notes: Appendix G derives these laws after neglecting disorder in Q; the true bias decays more slowly. R2–R4 additionally use the dominant high-temperature noise contribution, and the early-stopped error agrees only approximately with finite-size simulations.
